title: Strip a Value in Place
statement:
You get an integer array nums and a value val. Remove every occurrence of val from nums in place, without building a second array.

When you are done, nums must hold exactly the values that are not val, and nothing else: shrink it to the right length (in JavaScript set nums.length, in Python delete the tail). The kept values may end up in any order. Return nothing.

The classic version of this task returns the new length k and leaves junk after the first k slots. Here you trim the junk yourself, so the checker can see the result.

examples.why: Three 4s go. The two survivors move to the front, then the array is cut to length 2.
Every value matches, so nothing is left.
9 does not occur. The array keeps all its values.

hints: Deleting each match with splice shifts everything after it. Can you avoid shifting at all?
Keep a write index. Walk the array with a read index, and copy every value you want to keep to the write position.
After the walk, the first write slots hold the survivors. Cut the array to that length.

explain.intuition:
Removing matches one by one with splice costs O(n) each, because every later value shifts left. Instead, think of the array as two zones: the front part you have already decided to keep, and the rest you have not looked at yet.

A read pointer scans every value; a write pointer marks where the next kept value goes. Kept values get copied forward, matches are simply skipped. The write pointer never overtakes the read pointer, so nothing you still need gets overwritten. This is the same pattern as compacting a list of DOM nodes after filtering, just done on one array.
steps: For each index read: if nums[read] !== val, copy it to nums[write] and increment write.
Variant with fewer writes: when you see val, overwrite it with the last element and shrink by one, without advancing. Order changes, which is allowed.
pitfalls: Calling splice inside a forward loop and then incrementing the index. The element that slid into the current slot gets skipped.
Forgetting to trim. The tail still holds old values, so the array would contain more than the survivors.
In the swap-with-last variant, advancing past a slot right after filling it. The value that was moved in might also be val.

solutions.title: Read and write pointers
solutions.idea: Copy each kept value to the next write position, then cut the array at the write index. Keeps the original order.

solutions.title: Swap with the last element
solutions.idea: When a slot holds val, fill it with the last element and drop the last slot. Fewer writes when matches are rare; the order of survivors changes.

followups: Remove duplicates from a sorted array in place, keeping one of each. How does the write-pointer rule change?
Keep at most two copies of each value in a sorted array. What do you compare the new value against?
